prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and trade exposure reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: B027 answers a large question about who gains and loses from technology and trade, and does so with an explicit conceptual framework (the task approach and the race between education and technology) plus transparent identification (local labour-market exposure to import competition). That combination of framework and credible causal design is what I would apply to any candidate in any field. The core papers are one to three decades old, and replication, extension and critique have refined the findings without overturning the main results, so the work is mature. Its reach beyond labour economics is also evidence of consequence. It informs trade policy, adjustment policy and research on the political consequences of economic dislocation. Compared with the other candidates, the discovery is the easiest to state in a single citation, and I find the attribution cleaner than for B018, where credit is spread across eight names.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution under the three-name limit. The task framework and skill-premium work run through Autor and Katz, with other contributors (Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu, already recognised in 2024) outside the credited list. The China-shock identification is Autor, Dorn and Hanson, so any trio omits Dorn or Katz. The package may also be two prize-sized strands (technology and tasks, and trade shocks) joined by a common author. The long-run magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects remain debated, and the overlap with recent labour and technology prizes (Goldin 2023, Acemoglu 2024) could weaken the marginal case.

responses.point: Krusell proposes only Autor and Hanson for B027. He regards Katz and Dorn as important but separable, notes that Katz also appears under B028, and flags overlap with Acemoglu's task-based work. He also questions whether the shock papers are a conceptual advance or strong applied work.
responses.response: I agree that Autor and Hanson are the most defensible core. Autor spans both strands and Hanson anchors the trade-shock strand. I still keep Katz, because the skills-and-technology lineage is what gives the package its conceptual framework. Without Katz the citation would rest on the shock evidence alone, which is the part your question about conceptual advance applies to most. Katz also being credited under B028 does not, on the criteria I apply, reduce his contribution to the skill-demand literature, and I would not treat a name appearing on two ballots as a discount. The Acemoglu overlap is real. It is a reason to word the citation around the empirical demonstration of labour-market effects and not around the task model as theory.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B027 first with Autor, Dorn and Hanson. He argues the local labour-market effects of import competition are most cleanly credited to those three, while the task framework has wider authorship, and he accepts that excluding Katz is an attribution cost.
responses.response: We agree on the ranking and on the diagnosis. The disagreement is which cost to accept. If the citation were only about import competition, your trio would be the cleaner choice and I would find it hard to argue against. I prefer Katz over Dorn because I want the citation to cover the technology and skills side as well. That makes it broader than the China shock, and Autor links the two strands. I concede that Dorn's claim on the trade-shock papers is at least as strong as Hanson's co-origination claim. If the committee decides the citation should be narrowly about trade exposure, I would support your trio over mine.

responses.point: Hassler ranks B006 first and proposes Kiyotaki and Moore alone. He sees the collateral-constraint mechanism as a foundational building block of macro-finance, cleanly attributable to the originators and mature after nearly three decades. He treats the overlap with the 2022 prize as a possible redundancy.
responses.response: I accept that the attribution is cleaner than in my package, and a two-name award is easier to justify than a trio from four credited names. I rank B006 lower for two reasons. The contribution is mainly a theoretical mechanism whose direct empirical identification is thinner. The 2022 prize also covered adjacent ground, including the Bernanke-Gertler accelerator lineage. Neither is a disqualifier, but together they leave me less sure that the increment is as large as the one for B027. I would like to hear how you separate Kiyotaki-Moore from the 2022 work in a citation.

responses.point: Boppart ranks B001 first. He argues Mian and Sufi showed with granular data that household leverage drove the boom and the depth of the recession, that the 2022 prize did not cover the household-debt channel, and that the timing is ripe. He would exclude Campbell.
responses.response: I agree on excluding Campbell and on two names, since the work is overwhelmingly a Mian-Sufi partnership. I rank B001 third because the debate between credit-supply and expectations or demand-side interpretations is still live. I think a decade of evidence is somewhat less settled than for B027. I do not think your 'the 2022 prize did not cover the household channel' point is trivial, and it is a stronger answer to the redundancy worry than I gave credit for in my opening. B001 remains my first alternative to B012 if the committee wants a macro-finance award.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should credit Katz or Dorn as the third name, or restrict the citation to the trade-shock strand (Autor, Dorn, Hanson).
Whether the technology-and-tasks strand and the trade-shock strand are one discovery or two, and how much the 2023 and 2024 prizes reduce the marginal case.
How robust the China-shock magnitudes and persistence are, given later critiques and heterogeneity across countries.
Whether the opening support for B027 reflects the strength of the evidence or overlapping views; I cannot tell from the supplied documents and do not treat support counts as merit.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile for the B027 names or my alternatives (B012, B001). My field is political science, and B041 (Persson, Tabellini, Besley) is close to my home discipline, though it is not in my preferred configuration. I gave the 2024 presentation speech on the institutions prize, which is relevant to how I weigh B041, and I note it for transparency. I am a Stockholm University colleague of three committee members (Hassler, Krusell and Boppart), in a different department, and I list no co-authorship with any shortlisted candidate.
